item.title: Three weeks in Europe, part one: Madrid to Seville
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
Last year, my first trip to Europe was one week in Prague. This year I decided to make a little more of it. I am spending three weeks in Europe, starting in Madrid before heading to Seville for the annual Discourse company meetup.

I have been away from home for one week now. This is part one.

Portland to Madrid

I left Portland on September 20th and flew to Madrid through Dallas. I had only slept a few hours the night before because I thought being exhausted would help me sleep on the plane. That did not work nearly as well as I hoped.

We were already an hour late when we landed in Madrid, then it took another two hours to get off the plane and through customs. I had planned to take the train from the airport, but by then I was mostly trying to get to the hotel.

I did manage to get a Madrid Metro card. I learned later that I could have just tapped to pay.

I stayed at Hotel Artrip for three nights. The first day I got there, honestly, I slept through most of it.

Madrid might be the city that never sleeps

On my second day, I went to the center around Puerta del Sol and checked out the official Metro de Madrid store. It is a whole store for Madrid transit merchandise, which is exactly the sort of thing I will seek out while visiting a new city.

Madrid is a unique city. It might be the real city that never sleeps. It was busier at 3:30 in the morning outside my hotel than it was at 10 in the morning. I am not sure I could ever get used to the flow there.

For a person who likes documenting trips, I took exactly two pictures in Madrid. This was one of them:

On my last night, I met up with a coworker for pizza and gelato around Gran Vía, then took the Metro back to the hotel. I could not sleep and stayed up far too late even though I had a 9 a.m. train the next morning.

A much better way to travel

The other picture I took was at Madrid-Puerta de Atocha while waiting for the train to Seville.

The trip was scheduled for two hours and fifty minutes, but we arrived about ten minutes early. No one bought the seat next to me, which was a nice surprise. It was comfortable, easy, and made me wish the U.S. had a better rail system.

The long way to Triana

I went straight to Only YOU Hotel Sevilla and took a little siesta. After I got up, I walked around a bit and got a smoothie from Oakberry. Then I decided to walk around a little more to find coffee.

That turned into an hour-long walk to Muy Río, where I learned they had run out of filter coffee 45 minutes before closing. I gave up on coffee, but the walk ended up taking me right past Casa de Pilatos. I did not go inside because I was still on a coffee mission that had not officially failed yet.

Afterward, I crossed the Puente de Triana and walked around Triana looking at ceramics. Centro Cerámica Triana was closing soon, so I did not waste my money trying to rush through it. I hoped I would have time to come back.

I ate dinner at the hotel that night, and it was one of the top five meals of my life. I still need to get the names of the dishes. Somehow I found enough energy to go back out one more time for ice cream at Sibaris.

Transit cards and cake

I stayed up way too late again, slept until noon, and missed the hotel breakfast buffet.

My first task for the meetup was to get transit cards for the team. I rode the bus to Prado de San Sebastián and went to PAC Prado. After working through a little communication barrier, we did it. I left with the cards and decided to walk back to the hotel.

Later, I went to Cafetería Tartería Chanticream for queso con fresa and Muerte por Chocolate cakes with an espresso, then walked to the Setas de Sevilla. I got there around sunset and stayed long enough to watch the whole structure change as its lights came on.

On the walk home I took a picture of a random European street at night. That was apparently the theme of my photography for the day: giant wooden landmark, giant wooden landmark, giant wooden landmark, street.

Back to Triana

The next day I took the tram instead of walking or taking the bus. I finally got a decent filter coffee at Jester Coffee, then went back to Triana. This time I made it to Centro Cerámica Triana with enough time to visit the museum. I also bought a couple of tiles, because carrying fragile ceramics around Europe for another two weeks seemed like a good idea.

A lot of what caught my attention inside was ceramic being used as graphic design: advertisements, lettering, and public signs made out of tile.

Plaza de España

The next day I walked from the hotel to NYC Icy and got lotus and chocolate ice cream, then kept going to Plaza de España. It is a pretty sweet building and plaza. The whole place is full of ceramic and stone details that are easy to miss while looking at the scale of it.

The stonework was just as good. Someone cut a bow-tie-shaped joint directly into this railing, and I probably spent longer looking at it than any normal person would.

The downside was that all the carriage rides made the plaza smell like horse shit, especially with the temperature in the high 30s C.

That makes one week away from home. I have made it to Seville, figured out the transit, found the coffee, and bought breakable souvenirs far too early in the trip. The meetup is next.

Gracias por leer.

item.title: First time in Europe: One week in Prague
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
A Country Boy Goes to Europe

This past week was the annual global meetup for Discourse, the company I recently joined. I was lucky enough to get hired right before the planning cutoff date, and they were very generous to include me so early in my tenure. That inclusion made me feel valued and trusted. This year the meetup was held in Prague, Czech Republic. I was excited because I have never been out of North America.

Initial Leg and a Missed Connection in Amsterdam

The trip started with a flight from Portland to Amsterdam. It was pretty smooth, even if long. The only real issue was that the flight arrived late. On top of that, the passport control line in Amsterdam may have been the longest line I have ever seen in an airport. Those two things combined forced me to miss my connecting flight to Prague. Luckily I was flying KLM, which is very good about rebooking a new flight when it is their fault.

I had to do A LOT of walking and waiting, but I got rebooked and made it to my new flight.

Meeting My New Coworkers

For all the excitement, I was nervous too. I am introverted, and walking into a room of about 70 people I did not know was daunting. I am not great at introducing myself and I do not feel "important" enough to assume people want to meet me. I was not the only first timer, but I was by far the newest hire.

Prague Castle

Prague Castle is not a single building as much as it is a hilltop campus of courtyards, churches, palaces, and gardens.

St. Vitus Cathedral

Although I am anti-religion, I can appreciate the architecture of old world churches. Pictures cannot do this building justice. The height, beauty, and aging are things you just have to see in person.

Golden Lane (Zlatá ulička)

This pocket street sits between the Bílá Tower and Daliborka Tower. The tiny, colorful houses were built into the castle fortifications around the end of the 16th century and stayed lived in up to the Second World War. Several of the homes now show period interiors that trace everyday life on the lane across five centuries.

House No. 22 is the best known stop. Franz Kafka stayed here for a time during the First World War. Facades were repainted in the 1950s following designs by Jiří Trnka, which is part of why the lane looks so storybook today.

Climb the steps at House No. 12 to the terrace above Daliborka. The round tower dates to 1496 and served as a prison until 1781. You will see notes about the knight Dalibor of Kozojedy, the tower's first recorded inmate.

The Castle Proper (Old Royal Palace)

The Old Royal Palace centers on Vladislav Hall: huge, yet surprisingly open. The broad Riders' Staircase was built so horsemen could enter, which says a lot about the space's ambitions. Outside, the courtyards do the real work of the visit: sit, watch the guard change, and let the pace reset. On the south side, terraces step down toward the river with quiet garden paths and big sky views.

Public Trams-it

Prague's tram network is part moving museum, part everyday superpower.

A quick history:

  • 1875: horse trams debut in Prague
  • 1891: inventor František Křižík launches the first electric tram (Letná)
  • 1962: the Tatra T3, the red cream classic, begins service and becomes a design icon still seen today
  • 2010s to current: 100% low floor Škoda 15T ForCity sets the modern standard

I caught almost every ride at Veletržní palác, a 2 minute walk from Mama Shelter. Lines 6 and 17 stop here, so I could either hug the river or cut across town without thinking too hard. Daytime trams run about every 8 to 20 minutes, so it felt like show up and go.

Tram 6

Line 6 connects Nádraží Holešovice to Kubánské náměstí, which makes it a useful cross town link if you are moving between Holešovice, the center, and Vršovice. Daytime trams in Prague typically run every 8 to 20 minutes, so you can treat both 6 and 17 like show up and go service.

Tram 17

Line 17 hugs the Vltava for long stretches, so it is the easy, scenic way to glide past Národní divadlo, Staroměstská, Výtoň, and the riverfront. It links the north (Vozovna Kobylisy) with the south (Sídliště Modřany and Libuš). If you want a view rich ride, sit by the window on this one.

Czech Cubist Museum at The House of the Black Madonna

Czech Cubism did not stop at the canvas. It leapt into architecture, furniture, and everyday objects. One of the movement's showpieces is located at The House at the Black Madonna, which was built in 1911 to 1912 and designed by Josef Gočár. It was a Cubist designed department store turned cultural landmark of Old Town. Today it hosts The Museum of Czech Cubism and a restored Grand Cafe Orient.

Permanent Souvenirs

I decided to get a couple permanent souvenirs in the form of tattoos while there.

Tattoo by Dario Kristoffersen at One Love Tattoo. Prague, 2025.

Tattoo by Tarlito at One Love Tattoo. Prague, 2025.

Summary and Reflection

This was honestly the best trip of my life. I absolutely loved Prague and that old European energy. There was something different in the air. To me, it feels like a smaller, older New York City.

I loved it so much that I have already started a checklist for a digital nomad work visa. I could see going back for longer periods to visit and work. I regret not going to the transit museum, so that is high on the list for the next visit.

Děkuji, že jste si to přečetli.
